summary: A tentative proposal for a Unified User Level Protocol, intended to prompt discussion rather than serve as a rigorous specification. The author argues that using a different contact socket for each service, as FTP and RJE do, was unfortunate and unnecessary. He suggests a single approach built on Telnet.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of a different front door for every service, one author suggests using the same door and then saying what you want once inside.

questions: telnet as base for ftp proposal
telnet as base for protocol design
subtitle: A proposal to unify network protocols through a single Telnet connection.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET was developing separate protocols (FTP, RJEP) each with its own contact socket, creating architectural clutter and duplicating the work needed to implement connection handling for each new protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of multiple contact sockets, the Unified User Level Protocol (UULP) proposes that all user-level protocols flow through Telnet, with special control codes to indicate network generic functions. All protocols enter through the same connection point and use Telnet to negotiate their mode.
tldr.outcome: This was a discussion paper meant to prompt debate, not a specification. The idea influenced later thinking about protocol design, though the actual ARPANET and internet evolved with protocols like FTP using separate connections.

today: RFC 451 is a discussion paper that was not adopted as-is, yet it remains valuable as a record of thoughtful protocol design critique from the early ARPANET era. It influenced conversations about protocol architecture, though the internet evolved with protocols like FTP keeping separate connections. The paper's emphasis on architectural clarity and avoiding unnecessary complexity remains relevant to protocol design discussions.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
M. A. Padlipsky from MIT-Multics raises a concern about the ARPANET's approach to user-level protocols. The Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) allows defining a family of protocols by assigning each one a different contact socket—FTP has socket 3, RJEP has another, and others follow. Padlipsky argues this is "unfortunate and unnecessary," creating two problems.

First, each new protocol requires new mechanisms (processes, procedures, or patches) to handle incoming connections. This adds conceptual clutter. Second, there is confusion about whether protocols like FTP are just another layer of abstraction above Telnet or something fundamentally different. Padlipsky argues they should be unified.
sections.plainLanguage: Every service (file transfer, remote jobs, graphics) needs its own phone number to call. This seems wasteful when they all just want to send commands to a computer.

sections.title: The Unified User Level Protocol
sections.content:
Padlipsky notes that all existing user-level protocols already "speak Telnet"—they use Telnet or Telnet-like interactions. So why not extend this further? The UULP would have all users connect through Telnet as usual. When a user wants to perform a network generic function (like file transfer or job submission), they send a special Telnet Control Code indicating this, followed by the command.

The server's Telnet receiver sees the network generic function code and dispatches the command to the appropriate service handler. This preserves Telnet as the universal front door while allowing specialized protocols to operate behind it. A separate control code can indicate "unimplemented generic function," giving a cleaner way to report when a service is unavailable than having a socket close mean anything from "no server" to "server is busy."
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone dials the same Telnet number, then tells the computer 'I want to transfer files' or 'I want to run a job,' and it routes them to the right place.

sections.title: Design Elaborations
sections.content:
Padlipsky suggests refinements for implementation. Additional Telnet Control Codes could mark the beginning of specific protocols ("Begin FTP"), with the server responding with acknowledgment or "unimplemented." This helps systems that cannot dispatch input to separate processes still distinguish between local commands and protocol-specific ones. Alternative disciplines like those proposed in RFC 435 could be adopted.

One advantage of UULP is that all system capabilities—including password changing, which Braden noted was unavailable via FTP—become accessible through any protocol, since all capabilities come from the generic login. This avoids retrofitting features into individual protocols and reduces the "conceptual clutter" of having protocols operate in isolated universe of their own.

Padlipsky acknowledges that UULP may not be harder to implement than the current multiple contact socket approach, and contends that the advantages in extensibility and clarity make it worth considering.
sections.plainLanguage: The system could add extra signals to say 'I'm starting a file transfer now' or 'I'm beginning a job submission,' making it clearer what is happening and easier to add new services later.
